section.heading: 7.4 The Singular Value Decomposition
section.paragraph: The diagonalization theorems in Sections 5.3 and 7.1 play a part in many interesting applications. Unfortunately, as we know, not all matrices can be factored as $$A = PDP^{- 1}$$ with $$D$$ diagonal. However, a factorization $$A = Q D P^{- 1}$$ is possible for any $$m \times n$$ matrix $$A$$ ! A special factorization of this type, called the singular value decomposition, is one of the most useful matrix factorizations in applied linear algebra.

The singular value decomposition is based on the following property of the ordinary diagonalization that can be imitated for rectangular matrices: The absolute values of the eigenvalues of a symmetric matrix $$A$$ measure the amounts that $$A$$ stretches or shrinks certain vectors (the eigenvectors). If $$A\textbf{x} = \text{λ} \textbf{x}$$ and $$\text{∥} \textbf{x} \text{∥} = 1$$ , then
$$\parallel \textit{A} \textbf{x} \parallel = \parallel\lambda \textbf{x} \parallel = \left|\right. \lambda \left|\right. \parallel \textbf{x} \parallel = \left|\right. \lambda \left|\right.$$

If $$\text{λ} _{1}$$ is the eigenvalue with the greatest magnitude, then a corresponding unit eigenvector $$\textbf{v}_{1}$$ identifies a direction in which the stretching effect of $$A$$ is greatest. That is, the length of $$A\textbf{x}$$ is maximized when $$\textbf{x} = \textbf{v}_{1}$$ , and $$\left. \text{∥} \textit{A}\textbf{v}_{1} \text{∥} = \text{|λ} _{1} \right|$$ , by (1). This description of $$\textbf{v}_{1}$$ and $$\left| \text{λ} _{1} \right|$$ has an analogue for rectangular matrices that will lead to the singular value decomposition.

example.heading: Example 1
example.paragraph: If $$A = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{rrr} 4 & 11 & 14 \\ 8 & 7 & {- 2} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , then the linear transformation $$\textbf{x}\mapsto A\textbf{x}$$ maps the unit sphere $$\left\{ \textbf{x}: \text{∥} \textbf{x} \text{∥} = 1 \right\}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ onto an ellipse in $$\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ , shown in Figure 1. Find a unit vector $$\textbf{x}$$ at which the length $$\parallel A{\textbf{x} \parallel}$$ is maximized, and compute this maximum length.
example.heading: Figure 1
example.paragraph: A transformation from $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ to $$\mathbb{R}^{2}$$

image.alt: Two graphs show transforming a sphere on a three dimensional axis into an ellipse on a two dimensional axis.

example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: The quantity $$\text{∥} A{\textbf{x} \text{∥} }^{2}$$ is maximized at the same $$\textbf{x}$$ that maximizes $$\parallel A\textbf{x} \parallel$$ , and $$\parallel A\textbf{x} \parallel^{2}$$ is easier to study. Observe that
$$\parallel \textit{A} \textbf{x} \parallel^{2} = \left(( A \textbf{x} )\right)^{T} ( A \mathbf{x} ) = \textbf{x}^{T} A^{T} A \textbf{x} = \textbf{x}^{T} ( A^{T} A ) \textbf{x}$$

Also, $$A^{T} A$$ is a symmetric matrix, since $$(A^{T} A)^{T} = A^{T} A^{TT} = A^{T} A$$ . So the problem now is to maximize the quadratic form $$\textbf{x}^{T}\textbf{(}A^{T} A)\textbf{x}$$ subject to the constraint $$\text{∥} \textbf{x} \text{∥} = 1$$ . By Theorem 6 in Section 7.3, the maximum value is the greatest eigenvalue $$\text{λ} _{1}$$ of $$A^{T} A$$ . Also, the maximum value is attained at a unit eigenvector of $$A^{T}A$$ corresponding to $$\text{λ} _{1}$$ .
For the matrix $$A$$ in this example,

$$A^{T} A = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 8 \\ 11 & 7 \\ 14 & - 2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 11 & 14 \\ 8 & 7 & - 2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 80 & 100 & 40 \\ 100 & 170 & 140 \\ 40 & 140 & 200 \end{bmatrix}$$
The eigenvalues of $$A^{T}A$$ are $$\text{λ} _{1} = 360$$ , $$\text{λ} _{2} = 90$$ , and $$\text{λ} _{3} = 0$$ . Corresponding unit eigenvectors are, respectively,

$$\textbf{v}_{1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 / 3 \\ 2 / 3 \\ 2 / 3 \end{bmatrix} , \textbf{v}_{2} = \begin{bmatrix} - 2 / 3 \\ - 1 / 3 \\ 2 / 3 \end{bmatrix} , \textbf{v}_{3} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 / 3 \\ - 2 / 3 \\ 1 / 3 \end{bmatrix}$$

The maximum value of $$\parallel A{\textbf{x} \parallel}^{2}$$ is $$360$$ , attained when $$\textbf{x}$$ is the unit vector $$\textbf{v}_{1}$$ . The vector $$A\textbf{v}_{1}$$ is a point on the ellipse in Figure 1 farthest from the origin, namely
$$A \textbf{v}_{1} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 11 & 14 \\ 8 & 7 & - 2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 / 3 \\ 2 / 3 \\ 2 / 3 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 18 \\ 6 \end{bmatrix}$$
For $$\text{∥} \textbf{x} \text{∥} = 1$$ , the maximum value of $$\parallel A\textbf{x} \parallel$$ is $$\text{∥} \textit{A}\textbf{v}_{1} \text{∥} = \sqrt{360} = 6\sqrt{10}$$ .

section.paragraph: Example 1 suggests that the effect of $$A$$ on the unit sphere in $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ is related to the quadratic form $$\textbf{x}^{T}(A^{T}A)\textbf{x}$$ . In fact, the entire geometric behavior of the transformation $$\textbf{x}\mapsto A\textbf{x}$$ is captured by this quadratic form, as we shall see.
section.heading: The Singular Values of an m×n Matrix
section.paragraph: Let $$A$$ be an $$m \times n$$ matrix. Then $$A^{T}A$$ is symmetric and can be orthogonally diagonalized. Let $$\{\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{n}\}$$ be an orthonormal basis for $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ consisting of eigenvectors of $$A^{T}A$$ , and let $$\text{λ} _{1},\ldots, \text{λ} _{n}$$ be the associated eigenvalues of $$A^{T}A$$ . Then, for $$1 \leq i \leq n$$ ,

$$\parallel A \mathbf{v}_{i} \parallel^{2} & = & \left(( A \mathbf{v}_{i} )\right)^{T} A \mathbf{v}_{i} & = & \mathbf{v}_{i}^{T} A^{T} A \mathbf{v}_{i} & = & \mathbf{v}_{i}^{T} (\lambda_{i} \mathbf{v}_{i} ) & & \text{Since} \mathbf{v}_{i} \text{is} \text{an} \text{eigenvector} \text{of} A^{T} A & = & \lambda_{i} & & \text{Since} \mathbf{v}_{i} \text{is} \text{a} \text{unit} \text{vector}$$
So the eigenvalues of $$A^{T}A$$ are all nonnegative. By renumbering, if necessary, we may assume that the eigenvalues are arranged so that
$$\lambda_{1} \geq \lambda_{2} \geq \hdots \geq \lambda_{n} \geq 0$$

The singular values of $$A$$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of $$A^{T}A$$ , denoted by $$\sigma_{1},\ldots,\sigma_{n}$$ , and they are arranged in decreasing order. That is, $$\sigma_{i} = \sqrt{ \text{λ} _{i}}$$ for $$1 \leq i \leq n$$ . By equation (2), the singular values of $$A$$ are the lengths of the vectors $$A\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,A\textbf{v}_{n}$$ .

example.heading: Example 2
example.paragraph: Let $$A$$ be the matrix in Example 1. Since the eigenvalues of $$A^{T}A$$ are $$360$$ , $$90$$ , and $$0$$ , the singular values of $$A$$ are

From Example 1, the first singular value of $$A$$ is the maximum of $$\parallel A\textbf{x} \parallel$$ over all unit vectors, and the maximum is attained at the unit eigenvector $$\textbf{v}_{1}$$ . Theorem 7 in Section 7.3 shows that the second singular value of $$A$$ is the maximum of $$\parallel A\textbf{x} \parallel$$ over all unit vectors that are orthogonal to $$\textbf{v}_{1},$$ and this maximum is attained at the second unit eigenvector, $$\textbf{v}_{2}$$ (Exercise 22). For the $$\textbf{v}_{2}$$ in Example 1,
$$A \textbf{v}_{2} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 11 & 14 \\ 8 & 7 & - 2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} - 2 / 3 \\ - 1 / 3 \\ 2 / 3 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ - 9 \end{bmatrix}$$

This point is on the minor axis of the ellipse in Figure 1, just as $$A\textbf{v}_{1}$$ is on the major axis. (See Figure 2.) The first two singular values of $$A$$ are the lengths of the major and minor semiaxes of the ellipse.

image.alt: A graph shows an ellipse tilted towards the left.

section.paragraph: The fact that $$A\textbf{v}_{1}$$ and $$A\textbf{v}_{2}$$ are orthogonal in Figure 2 is no accident, as the next theorem shows.

note.title: Theorem 9
note.heading: Theorem 9
note.paragraph: Suppose $$\{\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{n}\}$$ is an orthonormal basis of $$\textbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ consisting of eigenvectors of $$A^{T}A$$ , arranged so that the corresponding eigenvalues of $$A^{T}A$$ satisfy $$\text{λ} _{1} \geq \cdots \geq \text{λ} _{n}$$ , and suppose $$A$$ has $$r$$ nonzero singular values. Then $$\{ A\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,A\textbf{v}_{r}\}$$ is an orthogonal basis for $$\text{Col} A$$ , and $$\text{rank} A = r$$ .

section.heading: Proof
section.paragraph: Because $$\textbf{v}_{i}$$ and $$\text{λ} _{j}\textbf{v}_{j}$$ are orthogonal for $$i \neq j$$ ,

$$\left(\right. A \textbf{v}_{i} \left.\right)^{T} \left(\right. A \textbf{v}_{j} \left.\right) = \textbf{v}_{i}^{T} A^{T} A \textbf{v}_{j} = \textbf{v}_{i}^{T} \left(\right. \lambda_{j} \textbf{v}_{j} \left.\right) = 0$$

Thus $$\{ A\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,A\textbf{v}_{n}\}$$ is an orthogonal set. Furthermore, since the lengths of the vectors $$A\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,A\textbf{v}_{n}$$ are the singular values of $$A$$ , and since there are $$r$$ nonzero singular values, $$A\textbf{v}_{i} \neq \textbf{0}$$ if and only if $$1 \leq i \leq r$$ . So $$A\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,A\textbf{v}_{r}$$ are linearly independent vectors, and they are in $$\text{Col} A$$ . Finally, for any $$\textbf{y}$$ in $$\text{Col} A$$ —say, $$\textbf{y} = A\textbf{x}$$ —we can write $$\textbf{x} = c_{1}\textbf{v}_{1} + \cdots + c_{n}\textbf{v}_{n}$$ , and

$$\textbf{y} & = A \textbf{x} = c_{1} A \textbf{v}_{1} + \hdots + c_{r} A \textbf{v}_{r} + c_{r + 1} A \textbf{v}_{r + 1} + \hdots + c_{n} A \textbf{v}_{n} & = c_{1} A \textbf{v}_{1} + \hdots + c_{r} A \textbf{v}_{r} + 0 + \hdots + 0$$

Thus $$\textbf{y}$$ is in $$\text{Span} \{ A\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,A\textbf{v}_{r}\}$$ , which shows that $$\{ A\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,A\textbf{v}_{r}\}$$ is an orthogonal basis for $$\text{Col} A$$ . Hence $$\text{rank} A = \dim \text{Col} A = r$$ .

note.title: Numerical Notes
note.heading: Numerical Notes
note.paragraph: In some cases, the rank of $$A$$ may be very sensitive to small changes in the entries of $$A$$ . The obvious method of counting the number of pivot columns in $$A$$ does not work well if $$A$$ is row reduced by a computer. Roundoff error often creates an echelon form with full rank.

In practice, the most reliable way to estimate the rank of a large matrix $$A$$ is to count the number of nonzero singular values. In this case, extremely small nonzero singular values are assumed to be zero for all practical purposes, and the effective rank of the matrix is the number obtained by counting the remaining nonzero singular values.1

section.paragraph: The decomposition of $$A$$ involves an $$m \times n$$ “diagonal” matrix $$\text{Σ}$$ of the form

note.title: Theorem 10
note.heading: Theorem 10
The Singular Value Decomposition
note.paragraph: Let $$A$$ be an $$m \times n$$ matrix with rank $$r$$ . Then there exists an $$m \times n$$ matrix $$\text{Σ}$$ as in (3) for which the diagonal entries in $$D$$ are the first $$r$$ singular values of $$A$$ , $$\sigma_{1} \geq \sigma_{2} \geq \cdots \geq \sigma_{r} > 0$$ , and there exist an $$m \times m$$ orthogonal matrix $$U$$ and an $$n \times n$$ orthogonal matrix $$V$$ such that

section.paragraph: Any factorization $$A = U \text{Σ} V^{T}$$ , with $$U$$ and $$V$$ orthogonal, $$\text{Σ}$$ as in (3), and positive diagonal entries in $$D$$ , is called a singular value decomposition (or SVD) of $$A$$ . The matrices $$U$$ and $$V$$ are not uniquely determined by $$A$$ , but the diagonal entries of $$\text{Σ}$$ are necessarily the singular values of $$A$$ . See Exercise 19. The columns of $$U$$ in such a decomposition are called left singular vectors of $$A$$ , and the columns of $$V$$ are called right singular vectors of $$A$$ .
section.heading: Proof
section.paragraph: Let $$\text{λ} _{i}$$ and $$\textbf{v}_{i}$$ be as in Theorem 9, so that $$\{ A\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,A\textbf{v}_{r}\}$$ is an orthogonal basis for $$\text{Col} A$$ . Normalize each $$A\textbf{v}_{i}$$ to obtain an orthonormal basis $$\{\textbf{u}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{u}_{r}\}$$ , where
$$\textbf{u}_{i} = \frac{1}{\parallel A \textbf{v}_{i} \parallel} A \textbf{v}_{i} = \frac{1}{\sigma_{i}} A \textbf{v}_{i}$$
and
$$A \textbf{v}_{i} = \sigma_{i} \textbf{u}_{i} \left(\right. 1 \leq i \leq r \left.\right)$$
Now extend $$\{\textbf{u}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{u}_{r}\}$$ to an orthonormal basis $$\{\textbf{u}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{u}_{m}\}$$ of $$\textbf{\mathbb{R}}^{m}$$ , and let
$$U = \left[\right. \textbf{u}_{1} & \textbf{u}_{2} & \hdots & \textbf{u}_{m} \left]\right. \text{and} V = \left[\right. \textbf{v}_{1} & \textbf{v}_{2} & \hdots & \textbf{v}_{n} \left]\right.$$
By construction, $$U$$ and $$V$$ are orthogonal matrices. Also, from (4),

$$A V = \left[\right. A \textbf{v}_{1} & \hdots & A \textbf{v}_{r} & 0 & \hdots & 0 \left]\right. = \left[\right. \sigma_{1} \textbf{u}_{1} & \hdots & \sigma_{r} \textbf{u}_{r} & 0 & \hdots & 0 \left]\right.$$
Let $$D$$ be the diagonal matrix with diagonal entries $$\sigma_{1},\ldots,\sigma_{r}$$ , and let $$\text{Σ}$$ be as in (3) above. Then

section.paragraph: Since $$V$$ is an orthogonal matrix, $$U \text{Σ} V^{T} = AVV^{T} = A$$ .

The next two examples focus attention on the internal structure of a singular value decomposition. An efficient and numerically stable algorithm for this decomposition would use a different approach. See the Numerical Note at the end of the section.

example.heading: Example 3
example.paragraph: Use the results of Examples 1 and 2 to construct a singular value decomposition of $$A = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{rrr} 4 & 11 & 14 \\ 8 & 7 & {- 2} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ .
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: A construction can be divided into three steps.

note.paragraph: STUDY GUIDE offers additional resources for learning to compute an SVD.

example.paragraph: Step 1. Find an orthogonal diagonalization of ﻿ $$\textit{\textbf{A}}^{\mathbf{T}}\textit{\textbf{A}}$$ That is, find the eigenvalues of ﻿ $$\textit{A}^{T}\textit{A}$$ and a corresponding orthonormal set of eigenvectors. If $$A$$ ﻿had only two columns, the calculations could be done by hand. Larger matrices usually require a matrix program. However, for the matrix $$A$$ here, the eigendata for $$A^{T} A$$ ﻿are provided in Example 1﻿.

Step 2. Set up $$\mathbf{\mathit{V}}$$ and ﻿ $$\Sigma$$ . Arrange the eigenvalues of ﻿ $$A^{T} A$$ in decreasing order. In Example 1, the eigenvalues are already listed in decreasing order: $$360$$ , $$90$$ , and $$0$$ . The corresponding unit eigenvectors, $$\mathbf{v}_{1}$$ ﻿, $$\mathbf{v}_{2}$$ ﻿, and $$\mathbf{v}_{3}$$ ﻿, are the right singular vectors of $$A$$ ﻿. Using Example 1, construct
$$V = \left[\textbf{v}_{1} \textbf{v}_{2} \textbf{v}_{3}\right] = \begin{bmatrix} 1 / 3 & - 2 / 3 & 2 / 3 \\ 2 / 3 & - 1 / 3 & - 2 / 3 \\ 2 / 3 & 2 / 3 & 1 / 3 \end{bmatrix}$$
The square roots of the eigenvalues are the singular values:
The nonzero singular values are the diagonal entries of $$D$$ . The matrix $$\text{Σ}$$ is the same size as $$A$$ , with $$D$$ in its upper left corner and with $$0$$ ’s elsewhere.
$$D = \left[\right. 6 \sqrt{10} & 0 0 & 3 \sqrt{10} \left]\right. , \Sigma = \left[\right. D & 0 \left]\right. = \left[\right. 6 \sqrt{10} & 0 & 0 0 & 3 \sqrt{10} & 0 \left]\right.$$

Step 3. Construct $$\mathbf{U}$$ . When ﻿ $$A$$ has rank ﻿ $$r$$ , the first $$r$$ columns of ﻿ $$U$$ are the normalized vectors obtained from $$A\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,A\textbf{v}_{r}$$ . In this example, $$A$$ has two nonzero singular values, so $$\text{rank} A = 2$$ . Recall from equation (2) and the paragraph before Example 2 that $$\text{∥} \textit{A}\textbf{v}_{1} \text{∥} = \sigma_{1}$$ and $$\text{∥} \textit{A}\textbf{v}_{2} \text{∥} = \sigma_{2}$$ . Thus

$$\mathbf{u}_{1} & = & \frac{1}{\sigma_{1}} A \mathbf{v}_{1} & = & \frac{1}{6 \sqrt{10}} \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}18 \\ 6\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} & = & \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}3 / \sqrt{10} \\ 1 / \sqrt{10}\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} \mathbf{u}_{2} & = & \frac{1}{\sigma_{2}} A \mathbf{v}_{2} & = & \frac{1}{3 \sqrt{10}} \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}3 \\ - 9\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} & = & \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}1 / \sqrt{10} \\ - 3 / \sqrt{10}\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix}$$

Note that $$\left\{ \textbf{u}_{1},\textbf{u}_{2} \right\}$$ ﻿ is already a basis for ﻿ $$\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ . Thus no additional vectors are needed for $$U$$ , and $$U = \left\lbrack \textbf{u}_{1} \textbf{u}_{2} \right\rbrack$$ . The singular value decomposition of ﻿ $$A$$ is

$$\begin{matrix}A & = & \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}3 / \sqrt{10} & 1 / \sqrt{10} \\ 1 / \sqrt{10} & - 3 / \sqrt{10}\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} & \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}6 \sqrt{10} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 \sqrt{10} & 0\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} & \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}1 / 3 & 2 / 3 & 2 / 3 \\ - 2 / 3 & - 1 / 3 & 2 / 3 \\ 2 / 3 & - 2 / 3 & 1 / 3\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} \\ & & \uparrow & \uparrow & \uparrow \\ & & U & \Sigma & V^{T}\end{matrix}$$

example.heading: Example 4
example.paragraph: Find a singular value decomposition of $$A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & - 1 \\ - 2 & 2 \\ 2 & - 2 \end{bmatrix} .$$
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: First, compute $$A^{T}A = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{rr} 9 & {- 9} \\ {- 9} & 9 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ . The eigenvalues of $$A^{T}A$$ are $$18$$ and $$0$$ , with corresponding unit eigenvectors
$$\textbf{v}_{1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 / \sqrt{2} \\ - 1 / \sqrt{2} \end{bmatrix} , \textbf{v}_{2} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 / \sqrt{2} \\ 1 / \sqrt{2} \end{bmatrix}$$
These unit vectors form the columns of $$V$$ :

$$V = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}\textbf{v}_{1} & \textbf{v}_{2}\end{matrix} \left]\right. = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}1 \sqrt{2} & 1 \sqrt{2} \\ - 1 \sqrt{2} & 1 \sqrt{2}\end{matrix} \left]\right.$$

The singular values are $$\sigma_{1} = \sqrt{18} = 3\sqrt{2}$$ and $$\sigma_{2} = 0$$ . Since there is only one nonzero singular value, the “matrix” $$D$$ may be written as a single number. That is, $$D = 3\sqrt{2}$$ . The matrix $$\text{Σ}$$ is the same size as $$A$$ , with $$D$$ in its upper left corner:
$$\Sigma = \left[\right. D & 0 0 & 0 0 & 0 \left]\right. = \left[\right. 3 \sqrt{2} & 0 0 & 0 0 & 0 \left]\right.$$
To construct $$U$$ , first construct $$A\textbf{v}_{1}$$ and $$A\textbf{v}_{2}$$ :
$$A \textbf{v}_{1} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 / \sqrt{2} \\ - 4 / \sqrt{2} \\ 4 / \sqrt{2} \end{bmatrix} , A \textbf{v}_{2} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}$$

As a check on the calculations, verify that $$\text{∥} A\textbf{v}_{1} \text{∥} = \sigma_{1} = 3\sqrt{2}$$ . Of course, $$A\textbf{v}_{2} = \textbf{0}$$ because $$\text{∥} \textit{A}\textbf{v}_{2} \text{∥} = \sigma_{2} = 0$$ . The only column found for $$U$$ so far is
$$\textbf{u}_{1} = \frac{1}{3 \sqrt{2}} A \textbf{v}_{1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 / 3 \\ - 2 / 3 \\ 2 / 3 \end{bmatrix}$$

The other columns of $$U$$ are found by extending the set $$\left\{ \textbf{u}_{1} \text{\}} \right.$$ to an orthonormal basis for $${\mathbb{R}}^{3}$$ . In this case, we need two orthogonal unit vectors $$\textbf{u}_{2}$$ and $$\textbf{u}_{3}$$ that are orthogonal to $$\textbf{u}_{1}$$ . (See Figure 3.) Each vector must satisfy $$\textbf{u}_{1}^{T}\textbf{x} = 0$$ , which is equivalent to the equation $$x_{1} - 2x_{2} + 2x_{3} = 0$$ . A basis for the solution set of this equation is
$$\textbf{w}_{1} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} , \textbf{w}_{2} = \begin{bmatrix} - 2 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$$

image.alt: A figure shows two circles on a two dimensional and a three dimensional graph.

example.paragraph: (Check that $$\textbf{w}_{1}$$ and $$\textbf{w}_{2}$$ are each orthogonal to $$\textbf{u}_{1}$$ .) Apply the Gram–Schmidt process (with normalizations) to $$\{\textbf{w}_{1},\textbf{w}_{2}\}$$ , and obtain
$$\textbf{u}_{2} = \left[\right. 2 / \sqrt{5} 1 / \sqrt{5} 0 \left]\right. , \textbf{u}_{3} = \left[\right. - 2 / \sqrt{45} 4 / \sqrt{45} 5 / \sqrt{45} \left]\right.$$
Finally, set $$U = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{rrr} \textbf{u}_{1} & \textbf{u}_{2} & \textbf{u}_{3} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , take $$\text{Σ}$$ and $$V^{T}$$ from above, and write

$$A = \left[\right. 1 & - 1 - 2 & 2 2 & - 2 \left]\right. = \left[\right. 1 / 3 & 2 / \sqrt{5} & - 2 / \sqrt{45} - 2 / 3 & 1 / \sqrt{5} & 4 / \sqrt{45} 2 / 3 & 0 & 5 / \sqrt{45} \left]\right. \left[\right. 3 \sqrt{2} & 0 0 & 0 0 & 0 \left]\right. \left[\right. 1 / \sqrt{2} & - 1 / \sqrt{2} 1 / \sqrt{2} & 1 / \sqrt{2} \left]\right.$$

section.heading: Applications of the Singular Value Decomposition
section.paragraph: The SVD is often used to estimate the rank of a matrix, as noted above. Several other numerical applications are described briefly below, and an application to image processing is presented in Section 7.5.

example.title: (The Condition Number)
example.heading: Example 5 (The Condition Number)
example.paragraph: Most numerical calculations involving an equation $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}$$ are as reliable as possible when the SVD of $$A$$ is used. The two orthogonal matrices $$U$$ and $$V$$ do not affect lengths of vectors or angles between vectors (Theorem 7 in Section 6.2). Any possible instabilities in numerical calculations are identified in $$\text{Σ}$$ . If the singular values of $$A$$ are extremely large or small, roundoff errors are almost inevitable, but an error analysis is aided by knowing the entries in $$\text{Σ}$$ and $$V$$ .

If $$A$$ is an invertible $$n \times n$$ matrix, then the ratio $$\sigma_{1}/\sigma_{n}$$ of the largest and smallest singular values gives the condition number of $$A$$ . Exercises 50–52 in Section 2.3 showed how the condition number affects the sensitivity of a solution of $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}$$ to changes (or errors) in the entries of $$A$$ . (Actually, a “condition number” of $$A$$ can be computed in several ways, but the definition given here is widely used for studying $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}$$ .)

example.title: (Bases for Fundamental Subspaces)
example.heading: Example 6 (Bases for Fundamental Subspaces)
example.paragraph: Given an SVD for an $$m \times n$$ matrix $$A$$ , let $$\textbf{u}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{u}_{m}$$ be the left singular vectors, $$\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{n}$$ the right singular vectors, and $$\sigma_{1},\ldots,\sigma_{n}$$ the singular values, and let $$r$$ be the rank of $$A$$ . By Theorem 9,
$$\left{\right. \textbf{u}_{1} , \ldots , \textbf{u}_{r} \left.\right}$$
is an orthonormal basis for $$\text{Col} A$$ .
Recall from Theorem 3 in Section 6.1 that $$\text{(Col} A)^{\bot} = \text{Nul} A^{T}$$ . Hence
$$\left{\right. \textbf{u}_{r + 1} , \ldots , \textbf{u}_{m} \left.\right}$$
is an orthonormal basis for $$\text{Nul} A^{T}$$ .

Since $$\text{∥} \textit{A}\textbf{v}_{i} \text{∥} = \sigma_{i}$$ for $$1 \leq i \leq n$$ , and $$\sigma_{i}$$ is $$0$$ if and only if $$i > r$$ , the vectors $$\textbf{v}_{r + 1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{n}$$ span a subspace of $$\text{Nul} A$$ of dimension $$n - r$$ . By the Rank Theorem, $$\dim \text{Nul} A = n - \text{rank} A$$ . It follows that
$$\left{\right. \textbf{v}_{r + 1} , \ldots , \textbf{v}_{n} \left.\right}$$
is an orthonormal basis for $$\text{Nul} A$$ , by the Basis Theorem (in Section 4.5).

From (5) and (6), the orthogonal complement of $$\text{Nul} A^{T}$$ is $$\text{Col} A$$ . Interchanging $$A$$ and $$A^{T}$$ , note that $$\text{(Nul} A)^{\bot} = \text{Col} A^{T} = \text{Row} A$$ . Hence, from (7),
$$\left{\right. \textbf{v}_{1} , \ldots , \textbf{v}_{r} \left.\right}$$
is an orthonormal basis for $$\text{Row} A$$ .

Figure 4 summarizes (5)–(8), but shows the orthogonal basis $$\{\sigma_{1}\textbf{u}_{1},\ldots,\sigma_{r}\textbf{u}_{r}\}$$ for $$\text{Col} A$$ instead of the normalized basis, to remind you that $$A\textbf{v}_{i} = \sigma_{i}\textbf{u}_{i}$$ for $$1 \leq i \leq r$$ . Explicit orthonormal bases for the four fundamental subspaces determined by $$A$$ are useful in some calculations, particularly in constrained optimization problems.

section.paragraph: The four fundamental subspaces and the concept of singular values provide the final statements of the Invertible Matrix Theorem. (Recall that statements about $$A^{T}$$ have been omitted from the theorem to avoid nearly doubling the number of statements.) The other statements were given in Sections 2.3, 2.9, 3.2, 4.5, and 5.2.

note.title: Theorem
note.heading: Theorem
The Invertible Matrix Theorem (concluded)
note.paragraph: Let $$A$$ be an $$n \times n$$ matrix. Then the following statements are each equivalent to the statement that $$A$$ is an invertible matrix:

example.title: (Reduced SVD and the Pseudoinverse of A)
example.heading: Example 7 (Reduced SVD and the Pseudoinverse of A)
example.paragraph: When $$\text{Σ}$$ contains rows or columns of zeros, a more compact decomposition of $$A$$ is possible. Using the notation established above, let $$r = \text{rank} A$$ , and partition $$U$$ and $$V$$ into submatrices whose first blocks contain $$r$$ columns:

$$U = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}U_{r} & U_{m - r}\end{matrix} \left]\right. , & \text{where} U_{r} = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}\textbf{u}_{1} & \hdots & \textbf{u}_{r}\end{matrix} \left]\right. V = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}V_{r} & V_{n - r}\end{matrix} \left]\right. , & \text{where} V_{r} = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}\textbf{v}_{1} & \hdots & \textbf{v}_{r}\end{matrix} \left]\right.$$

Then $$U_{r}$$ is $$m \times r$$ and $$V_{r}$$ is $$n \times r$$ . (To simplify notation, we consider $$U_{m - r}$$ or $$V_{n - r}$$ even though one of them may have no columns.) Then partitioned matrix multiplication shows that
$$A = \left[\right. U_{r} & U_{m - r} \left]\right. \left[\right. D & 0 0 & 0 \left]\right. \left[\right. V_{r}^{T} V_{n - r}^{T} \left]\right. = U_{r} D V_{r}^{T}$$

This factorization of $$A$$ is called a reduced singular value decomposition of $$A$$ . Since the diagonal entries in $$D$$ are nonzero, $$D$$ is invertible. The following matrix is called the pseudoinverse (also, the Moore–Penrose inverse) of $$A$$ :
Supplementary Exercises 28–30 at the end of the chapter explore some of the properties of the reduced singular value decomposition and the pseudoinverse.

example.title: (Least-Squares Solution)
example.heading: Example 8 (Least-Squares Solution)
example.paragraph: Given the equation $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}$$ , use the pseudoinverse of $$A$$ in (10) to define
$$\hat{\textbf{x}} = A^{+} \textbf{b} = V_{r} D^{- 1} U_{r}^{T} \textbf{b}$$
Then, from the SVD in (9),

$$A \hat{\textbf{x}} & = \left(\right. U_{r} D V_{r}^{T} \left.\right) \left(\right. V_{r} D^{- 1} U_{r}^{T} \textbf{b} \left.\right) & = U_{r} \left(D D\right)^{- 1} U_{r}^{T} \textbf{b} \text{Because} V_{r}^{T} V_{r} = I_{r} & = U_{r} U_{r}^{T} \textbf{b}$$

It follows from (5) that $$U_{r}U_{r}^{T}\textbf{b}$$ is the orthogonal projection $$\widehat{\textbf{b}}$$ of $$\textbf{b}$$ onto $$\text{Col} A$$ . (See Theorem 10 in Section 6.3.) Thus $$\widehat{\textbf{x}}$$ is a least-squares solution of $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}$$ . In fact, this $$\widehat{\textbf{x}}$$ has the smallest length among all least-squares solutions of $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}$$ . See Supplementary Exercise 30.

note.title: Numerical Notes
note.heading: Numerical Notes
note.paragraph: Examples 1–4﻿ and the exercises illustrate the concept of singular values and suggest how to perform calculations by hand. In practice, the computation of $$A^{T} A$$ should be avoided, since any errors in the entries of $$A$$ are squared in the entries of $$A^{T} A$$ . There exist fast iterative methods that produce the singular values and singular vectors of $$A$$ accurately to many decimal places.

note.title: Practice Problems
note.heading: Practice Problems

list.item: Given a singular value decomposition, $$A = U \text{Σ} V^{T}$$ , find an SVD of $$A^{T}$$ . How are the singular values of $$A$$ and $$A^{T}$$ related?
For any $$n \times n$$ matrix $$A$$ , use the SVD to show that there is an $$n \times n$$ orthogonal matrix $$Q$$ such that $$A^{T} A = Q^{T}(A^{T} A)Q$$ .

note.paragraph: Remark: Practice Problem 2 establishes that for any $$n \times n$$ matrix $$A$$ , the matrices $$AA^{T}$$ and $$A^{T} A$$ are orthogonally similar.
